Stellar mass determination (M1​+M2​=4π2a3/(GP2))

Words: 66
Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Orbital dynamics gives the most direct stellar masses: a resolved binary orbit and distance determine the relative semimajor axis, and Kepler's third law gives the total mass. The barycentric size or radial-velocity amplitude ratio gives individual masses. An eclipsing binary inclination removes the sine-cubed projection factor from spectroscopic masses; a single-lined binary mass function alone does not uniquely determine both masses. Surface-gravity/radius and stellar-track estimates are model-dependent and are calibrated against dynamical binary measurements.

Mass loss (astrophysics, M˙<0)

Words: 51
Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Loss of matter from a star or other astronomical system, for example through a stellar wind or explosive ejection. Mass loss rate conventions must distinguish the positive ejected rate ∣M˙∣ from the negative change of the retained mass, M˙. In a binary star, the fate of an orbit also depends on the specific angular momentum carried away.

Stellar rotation (Ω(r,θ))

Words: 140 Articles: 2
Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
The spin of a star about its axis, which can be solid-body rotation or vary through the interior. Angular momentum transport and rotational mixing can change the stellar composition profile and available fuel. An observed surface rotation rate does not determine the entire interior profile.

Gyroscopic pumping in a star (ρvm​⋅∇(ϖ2Ω)=−∇⋅FJ​)

Words: 51
Stellar rotation OurBigBook.com
In a steady axisymmetric star, a torque due to Reynolds stress, Maxwell stress tensor or viscosity must balance advection of specific angular momentum by stellar meridional circulation. Writing the nonadvective angular momentum transport flux as FJ​ gives the displayed balance. Thus stresses that maintain differential rotation also drive a meridional response. The stellar thermal-wind balance supplies a separate leading force constraint, not a replacement for this torque equation.

Stellar thermal-wind balance (ϖ∂z​Ω2=rcp​g​∂θ​S)

Words: 52
Stellar rotation OurBigBook.com
Taking the curl of axisymmetric hydrostatic equilibrium with centrifugal acceleration gives ϖ∂z​Ω2=(∇p×∇ρ)ϕ​/ρ2. For an approximately spherical ideal gas with constant composition, use ∇ρ=∇p/cs2​−ρ∇S/cp​ to obtain the displayed relation. Latitudinal entropy differences can support noncylindrical differential rotation. A barotropic fluid gives cylindrical rotation in this leading balance; the relation does not determine the transport stresses or circulation rate.

Stellar gravity (GM⋆​/r2)

Words: 23
Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
Outside a spherical star, its gravitational acceleration is −GM⋆​r/r3. It provides the dominant central force for Kepler orbits in a star-dominated planetary system.

Stellar population

Words: 279 Articles: 6
Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
A stellar population is an ensemble of stars described by its formation times, initial masses, composition and present stellar evolution states. Number fractions must be distinguished from mass-weighted fractions. Shared formation times can correlate the states of components of a binary star even when their initial masses have independence.

Population III star

Words: 32
Stellar population OurBigBook.com
A Population III star is a first-generation star formed from essentially metal-free primordial gas. Limited cooling generally raises its characteristic fragmentation mass and favors a more top-heavy initial mass function than in enriched star formation.

Population II star

Words: 35
Stellar population OurBigBook.com
A Population II star is an old metal-poor star formed from gas enriched by earlier stellar generations. Metal and dust cooling let enriched gas fragment to lower masses than primordial gas under otherwise comparable conditions.

Age-metallicity degeneracy

Words: 44
Stellar population OurBigBook.com
Integrated spectra can confuse older stellar populations with more metal-rich ones because both can redden the light and change absorption lines. Line strengths depend on stellar metallicity, temperatures, ages, and abundance ratios. Weak metal lines in a young population dominated by hot bright stars need not indicate low stellar metallicity.

Evolutionary-state selection by stellar lifetimes

Words: 79 Articles: 1
Stellar population OurBigBook.com
Given a birth-mass distribution and age distribution, an evolutionary state occupies the mass-age set where its starting lifetime has elapsed and its ending lifetime has not. The state number fraction is the probability measure of this set. Initial mass function tail coordinates and the probability integral transform can turn these weighted regions into simple geometric areas.

Stellar lifetime regions in a mass-age diagram (τa​(M)<t<τb​(M))

Words: 30
Evolutionary-state selection by stellar lifetimes OurBigBook.com
A phase bounded by mass-dependent lifetimes τa​(M) and τb​(M) occupies τa​(M)<t<τb​(M), clipped to the population age range. Its boundaries can be mapped into uniform probability coordinates to evaluate evolutionary-state fractions.

Birth-age distribution under constant star formation (Y(t)=t/T(0≤t≤T))

Words: 45
Stellar population OurBigBook.com
If a population forms at a constant number rate for duration T and every birth object is retained in the census, its present ages are uniform on [0,T]. A fixed initial mass function with finite mean birth mass also makes constant mass-based star formation rate equivalent to constant number rate.

Stellar atmosphere

Words: 507 Articles: 10
Stellar astrophysics OurBigBook.com
A stellar atmosphere is the outer region that determines the escaping spectrum and matches the interior stellar structure to its radiation boundary conditions. A photosphere is the layer near unit optical depth, not a zero-temperature boundary. The inward intensity at the outer surface vanishes when there is no external illumination.

Stellar chemical abundance (Xi​,ni​/nH​)

The solar magnetic field is generated and maintained by electrically conducting flows through solar dynamo action. ∂t​B=∇×(U×B+E−η∇×B),
(1)

Rotation influences convection, its helicity and differential rotation, which feed dynamo action. Wind braking lowers the rotation rate and ordinarily reduces unsaturated activity. Lorentz force feedback also changes the differential rotation and convective motions, saturating the dynamo on shorter time scales. Secular evolution, cyclic polarity reversal and irregular modulation are distinct time scales of this coupled system.

Thus a toroidal field that produces rising bipolar regions feeds back into a poloidal magnetic field. A sunspot is a relatively cool, dark photospheric region associated with concentrated magnetic flux. Their number and latitude distribution are visible tracers of the solar cycle.

Sunspot OurBigBook.com
The axis of a bipolar solar active region is statistically tilted relative to the local east-west direction, with its following polarity typically farther from the equator and a mean tilt that grows with latitude. Scatter is substantial. The separation in latitude of the two polarities allows their surface dispersal to generate a net poloidal field through the Babcock-Leighton mechanism.

The solar cycle is the recurrent variation of magnetic activity, with a characteristic sunspot-number period of about eleven years. The large-scale magnetic polarity reverses from one activity cycle to the next, giving an approximately twenty-two-year magnetic cycle. Activity cycles vary in length and amplitude. A satisfactory solar dynamo model must account for polarity reversal, equatorward activity-belt migration in the solar butterfly diagram, the phase relation between polar and active-region fields, and long-term modulation including solar grand minima.

A solar grand minimum is a prolonged interval, lasting several ordinary cycles, of strongly reduced sunspot activity. Historical records identify the Maunder minimum; cosmogenic carbon-14 and beryllium-10 provide longer indirect records because stronger heliospheric magnetic shielding generally reduces cosmic-ray production of these isotopes. Weak activity does not imply a zero solar magnetic field. Proposed causes include stochastic weakening of poloidal-field generation, nonlinear dynamo modulation, and intermittency near an excitation threshold.

The Maunder minimum is the interval approximately 1645–1715 when recorded sunspot activity was exceptionally low. It is the best-known historical solar grand minimum. Bipolar solar active regions preferentially have one leading magnetic polarity in a given hemisphere and cycle, the opposite leading polarity in the other hemisphere, and reversed assignments in the next cycle. The diagram constrains both Parker dynamo wave propagation and magnetic transport in flux-transport solar dynamos.

Weaker events can produce pulses rather than full disruption, and still heavier cores can collapse without an explosion. Thus the thermal relativity scale alone neither establishes the instability nor predicts its outcome.

Proton-proton chain branches (pp I, pp II, pp III)

Words: 449 Articles: 7
Proton–proton chain OurBigBook.com
The proton–proton chain first produces deuterium by a weak reaction and then helium-3 by proton capture. pp I ends with 3He+3He→4He+2p. pp II passes through beryllium-7 electron capture to lithium-7 and then proton capture. pp III passes through boron-8 beta-plus decay and beryllium-8 breakup. Each branch produces one net helium-4 nucleus from four protons, but the neutrino spectrum and deposited heat differ. In pp II the net weak reactions involve one emitted positron and one captured electron.

Proton-proton chain branches OurBigBook.com
Present solar hydrogen is most depleted in the central burning region and rises toward the envelope. helium-3 is efficiently destroyed in the hot centre, increases outward as its equilibrium abundance rises, and develops an off-centre maximum where equilibration becomes slow. Still farther out its production becomes weak, leaving a smaller envelope abundance. Convective mixing tends to flatten the outer profiles. This qualitative pattern is not itself a quantitative solar model.

The weighted baryon mass density n1​+2n2​+3n3​+4n4​+7n7​ is conserved by the nuclear reactions at fixed volume.

A branch of the CNO cycle proceeds through proton captures on nitrogen-15 and oxygen-16, beta-plus decay of fluorine-17, and 17O(p,α)14N. Returning through oxygen-15 and nitrogen-15 closes the cycle. The stellar thermostat is the negative feedback between temperature-sensitive nuclear burning and hydrostatic expansion: excess burning expands and cools a star, while deficient burning permits contraction and heating.

Core helium burning begins when a hydrogen-exhausted stellar core becomes hot enough for the Triple-alpha process. Subsequent alpha capture on carbon produces oxygen, leaving a carbon-oxygen core after central helium exhaustion.

A helium flash is a thermally unstable ignition of helium in an electron-degenerate stellar core. A nondegenerate intermediate-mass core can expand and regulate ignition, so a usual isolated star of five solar masses begins core helium burning without this flash.

The slow neutron-capture process builds nuclei heavier than iron when neutron captures occur more slowly than typical beta decays. Thermal pulses in asymptotic-giant-branch stars produce characteristic enhancements of elements such as strontium, zirconium, and barium.

Main-sequence turnoff

Main sequence OurBigBook.com
The main-sequence turnoff is the location in a coeval population's Hertzsprung-Russell diagram where stars are leaving the main sequence after exhausting their core hydrogen. More massive stars generally have larger luminosity per unit mass and shorter nuclear lifetimes, so the most massive stars still on the main sequence constrain the population's age. In a simple model, equating the stellar nuclear timescale t∼qM/L(M) to the common age determines a turnoff mass; detailed calibration requires composition and stellar models.

Post-asymptotic giant branch evolution

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
After substantial envelope loss on the Asymptotic giant branch, a low- or intermediate-mass star's exposed core heats while its radius shrinks, often at approximately constant luminosity during continued shell burning. It may ionize the expelled envelope as a planetary nebula. After the remaining nuclear fuel is depleted, its luminosity decreases and it joins a white dwarf cooling track. Evolutionary tracks on the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram connect the central-star temperature and luminosity with core mass and elapsed time.

Stellar nuclear timescale (tnuc​∼Efuel​/L)

Words: 67
Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
The time for stellar nuclear fusion to consume the accessible fuel at characteristic luminosity L. If a fraction f of a star's mass M supplies fuel abundance X and released energy per unit fuel mass EH​, hydrogen burning gives tnuc​∼fXMEH​/L. Accessible core fuel, rather than the entire star, sets the lifetime unless mixing is complete. This is longer than a structural Kelvin-Helmholtz cooling time when the nuclear reservoir greatly exceeds the gravitational contraction reservoir.

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
A stellar remnant is the object left after a star finishes its principal nuclear-burning evolution, such as a white dwarf, neutron star or black hole. Stellar remnants retain mass while often contributing little optical light, affecting an old stellar population's mass-to-light ratio.

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
The stellar age is the elapsed time since a star formed. A constant number formation rate on a finite interval gives a uniform distribution of present ages if every formed object remains counted, including stellar remnants. An age distribution inferred only from surviving main sequence stars generally differs because their lifetimes depend on mass.

If ΦE0​​(T)=∫E0​/h∞​Bν​(T)/(hν)dν, then [Fℓ​/(hνℓ​Fνo​,∗​)][β/αℓeff​]=ΦE0​​(Ts​)/Bνo​​(Ts​) when the line traces the full appropriate ionizing budget. Both the distance and stellar radius cancel. Density inhomogeneity also cancels from the integrated recombination estimate when the coefficient ratio is known; photon leakage, dust and mixed-species transfer can invalidate the simple budget.

Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism

Stellar evolution OurBigBook.com
Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction releases gravitational binding energy as a self-gravitating body cools and shrinks. It powers young stars and giant planets before nuclear burning or degeneracy dominates their thermal evolution.

Words: 67
Kelvin-Helmholtz mechanism OurBigBook.com
For a monatomic gas obeying the ideal gas law, the specific internal energy is e=3P/(2ρ). With no stellar nuclear fusion heating, the first law of thermodynamics makes the effective stellar energy-generation rate ϵ=−∂t​e−P∂t​(1/ρ), with the derivatives taken at fixed enclosed mass. Differentiating gives ϵ=−3∂t​P/(2ρ)+5P∂t​ρ/(2ρ2). In a fixed-mass stellar homology Kelvin-Helmholtz contraction, ρ∝R−3 and P∝R−4 at each mass label. Hence ϵ=−3PR˙/(2ρR)>0 when R˙<0. This includes internal energy storage as well as pressure work; using the gravitational potential-energy decrease alone would overestimate the outgoing luminosity.

The intrinsic planetary luminosity Lint​ is the power supplied by interior cooling, contraction, nuclear reactions if present, or internal heating, excluding reflected or passively reradiated stellar light. For fixed mass and no accretion or nuclear source, global conservation of energy gives Lint​=Qdeep​−d(U+Ω)/dt, where Qdeep​ is any additional power deposited in the interior, such as tidal heating or Joule heating. For Qdeep​=0 and a gas-supported quasi-static sphere of fixed specific-heat ratio γ and negligible surface pressure, the stellar virial theorem gives Ω=−3(γ−1)U, hence
Lint​=−3(γ−1)3γ−4​dtdΩ​.
(5)
For a dynamically stable gas-supported model take γ>4/3. For γ=5/3 this is half the gravitational release. Degenerate giants require a different internal energy reservoir; the half-factor is not universal.

A binary star is a gravitationally bound pair orbiting their common centre of mass.

A Type I X-ray burst is a transient thermonuclear runaway in accreted hydrogen or helium on a neutron star surface. It rises rapidly and cools after the fuel burns. In Jeans-mode mass loss, an isotropic wind escapes from one binary component carrying that star's specific orbital angular momentum. If the companion accretes negligibly, a circular binary obeys aM=constant and PM2=constant.

A barium star is a main-sequence or giant star enriched in carbon and slow-neutron-capture elements despite being too unevolved to have made them itself. It was polluted by an asymptotic-giant-branch companion that is now a white dwarf.

An S-type star has strong zirconium-oxide bands and enhanced slow-neutron-capture elements. Intrinsic S-type stars are thermally pulsing asymptotic giants, while extrinsic S-type stars were polluted by a former asymptotic-giant-branch companion.

Binary star OurBigBook.com
A cataclysmic variable is a close binary in which a Roche-lobe-filling low-mass star transfers matter to a white dwarf. Angular-momentum loss drives long-term transfer, while unstable burning of accumulated hydrogen produces classical novae.

Cataclysmic variable OurBigBook.com
A cataclysmic variable whose persistent luminous disk resembles a dwarf nova in outburst. A sufficiently high transfer rate can keep its accretion disk on the hot stable branch of the hydrogen-ionization disk instability, avoiding ordinary dwarf-nova cycles.

Cataclysmic variable OurBigBook.com
A cataclysmic variable with recurrent disk outbursts associated with the hydrogen-ionization disk instability. Enhanced accretion powers the bright phase; the event does not require thermonuclear runaway on the white dwarf.

Cataclysmic variable OurBigBook.com
A cataclysmic variable whose white dwarf magnetic field does not dominate the large-scale accretion flow. It normally supports an accretion disk fed through Roche-lobe overflow. The term does not rule out a magnetized donor star or magnetic braking of a binary star.

Nonmagnetic cataclysmic variable OurBigBook.com
The bright region where the stream from Roche-lobe overflow strikes an accretion disk. Dissipation of relative kinetic energy produces a localized source of light whose visibility changes around the orbital period.

Cataclysmic variable OurBigBook.com
Ordinary hydrogen-rich cataclysmic variables occur on both sides of a cataclysmic-variable period gap at approximately two to three hours, with a cataclysmic-variable period minimum near 82 minutes. Selection effects change the observed proportions. Knigge, Baraffe and Patterson's donor-based evolutionary study summarizes these empirical landmarks.
Cataclysmic-variable period minimum (Pmin​)
Words: 105 Articles: 1
Cataclysmic-variable orbital-period distribution OurBigBook.com
For a Roche lobe-filling donor with local radius response R2​∝M2ζ​, the Roche-lobe-filling period-density relation gives P∝M2(3ζ−1)/2​. As mass is lost, the period falls for ζ>1/3 and rises for ζ<1/3, with a minimum at the transition. The reversal is called a period bounce. Slow evolution near the turning point produces an accumulation in the period distribution: for a steady flow of systems along one evolutionary branch, N(P)∝1/∣P˙∣.
Cataclysmic-variable period bounce (ζ=1/3)

Cataclysmic-variable period minimum OurBigBook.com
The reversal from decreasing to increasing orbital period during continuing donor mass loss. The Roche-lobe-filling period-density relation gives dlogP/dlogMd​=(3ζ−1)/2, where ζ is the effective stellar radius response exponent along the mass-losing sequence. A crossing from ζ>1/3 to ζ<1/3 gives a local cataclysmic-variable period minimum.

Cataclysmic-variable orbital-period distribution OurBigBook.com
The cataclysmic-variable period gap is the observed deficit of accreting, ordinary hydrogen-rich cataclysmic variables with periods around two to three hours. The disrupted magnetic braking model interprets it as a detached phase after the donor contracts inside its Roche lobe.

Magnetic braking of a binary star

Words: 95 Articles: 1
Cataclysmic variable OurBigBook.com
A magnetized wind removes spin angular momentum from a cool donor star. Tidal synchronization replenishes that spin from the orbit, so the wind indirectly removes orbital angular momentum and drives the binary toward shorter separation.
Disrupted magnetic braking model
Words: 60
Magnetic braking of a binary star OurBigBook.com
In this model, strong magnetic braking of a binary star inflates the mass-losing donor above the cataclysmic-variable period gap. A reduction in the torque near the fully convective star transition allows thermal contraction and detachment. Gravitational-wave emission from a binary system continues to shrink the orbit until contact returns below the gap. The model requires a braking decrease and a previously inflated donor, not disappearance of stellar magnetism. Knigge's review describes this evolutionary picture and observational tests.

In isotropic re-emission, transferred mass is expelled from the vicinity of the accretor and carries the accretor's specific orbital angular momentum. The total binary mass and orbital angular momentum then decrease even though the accretor retains no net mass.

Words: 122 Articles: 1
Supernova kick in a binary star OurBigBook.com
For an impulsive supernova kick in a binary star initially in a circular Kepler orbit, let β be the remaining total mass fraction and α the kick speed divided by the original relative speed. The displayed post-kick specific orbital energy is negative for a bound pair and positive for escape. Over all directions, the velocity factor ranges from (1−α)2 to (1+α)2. Some direction leaves a bound pair exactly when 2β>(1−α)2; some direction permits positive-energy escape exactly when 2β<(1+α)2. Equalities are marginal parabolic Kepler orbits. The circular initial orbit and impulsive approximation are essential.

A common-envelope phase occurs when unstable binary interaction engulfs both stellar cores in one envelope. Orbital energy and angular momentum may eject the envelope, leaving a compact binary, or the cores may merge.

The common-envelope energy formalism equates a fraction αCE​ of the released orbital energy to the envelope binding energy, often written Ebind​=GMd​Menv​/(λRd​). It estimates the post-envelope separation but compresses uncertain hydrodynamics into αCE​ and λ.

The double-degenerate scenario forms a close pair of carbon--oxygen white dwarfs, usually through mass transfer and one or more common-envelope phases. Gravitational radiation then shrinks the orbit until merger or unstable transfer triggers thermonuclear disruption.

An Algol binary is a semidetached binary in which an evolved, less massive donor star fills its Roche lobe while its more massive mass gainer remains near the main sequence. Binary mass-ratio reversal resolves the Algol paradox. Eclipsing members commonly have Algol variable light curves, but that observational class also includes detached systems.
Algol paradox
Words: 41
Algol binary OurBigBook.com
The Algol paradox is the apparently inconsistent evolutionary ordering in an Algol binary: the less massive star is more evolved, whereas higher-mass isolated main sequence stars normally exhaust core fuel sooner. Binary mass-ratio reversal resolves it by identifying the present donor as the initially more massive star.
Binary mass-ratio reversal
Words: 50
Algol binary OurBigBook.com
During binary mass-ratio reversal, an initially more massive donor star loses enough material that its companion becomes the more massive member. The stars retain their different prior nuclear evolution, resolving the Algol paradox. Conservative binary mass transfer shrinks the orbit before equal masses and widens it after reversal, because a∝(Md​Ma​)−2 at fixed total mass and orbital angular momentum.
Algol mass-ratio stability limit (qcrit​≃2/3)
Words: 63
Algol binary OurBigBook.com
A simplified conservative model with a fully convective donor gives long-lived stable Roche-lobe overflow only for donor-to-accretor mass ratio q<2/3. This follows from the Roche-lobe radius response exponent and the donor's adiabatic stellar radius response exponent −1/3. The boundary is model-dependent; radiative donors, evolved core structure and mass or angular-momentum loss change it. Van Rensbergen and collaborators' Algol population study includes reported Algol mass ratios above 0.7 and discusses observational uncertainties.
